title: 2 Chronicles 21:8–20
context: Edom and Libnah revolt because Jehoram has forsaken the LORD, and he leads Judah into idolatry. A letter from Elijah, found only in Chronicles, announces judgment on his household and a severe illness. The LORD stirs up the Philistines and Arabians, who carry off his possessions and all his sons but the youngest, and Jehoram dies of the illness, unmourned and buried outside the kings’ tombs. The parallel in 2 Kings 8:20–24 is much shorter. The notes handle the murder, the letter, and the illness soberly. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about judgment and the certainty of God’s word.

verses.text: In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah, and made a king over themselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
In Jehoram’s days Edom revolts from Judah’s hand and sets up its own king. The verse matches 2 Kings 8:20.

Arminian readers see the loss of Edom as a consequence of Jehoram’s unfaithful reign, as the narrative will make explicit in verse 10.
verses.reformedNotes:
Edom had been subject since David’s day, according to earlier narratives (2 Samuel 8:14).

Reformed readers see God loosening Judah’s hold as discipline. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the effects of the king’s sin on the kingdom.

verses.text: Then Jehoram went there with his captains and all his chariots with him. He rose up by night and struck the Edomites who surrounded him, along with the captains of the chariots.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoram goes with his captains and chariots, rises by night, and strikes the Edomites surrounding him. The battle seems to be an escape more than a victory.

Arminian readers see a king unable to reverse the revolt.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 8:21 names Zair and adds that the people fled to their tents; Chronicles omits both. The details of the battle are not fully clear in either account.

Reformed readers see limited success under discipline. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: So Edom has been in revolt from under the hand of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time from under his hand, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
Edom remains in revolt to this day, and Libnah revolts too, because Jehoram has forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers. The narrator gives the reason.

Arminian readers see covenant consequences following a free choice to forsake God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles adds the explanation that 2 Kings 8:22 does not give. Libnah’s exact location is debated, though it appears to have lain in Judah’s lowland.

Reformed readers see God’s discipline explained by his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Moreover he made high places in the mountains of Judah, and made the inhabitants of Jerusalem play the prostitute, and led Judah astray.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoram makes high places in Judah’s hill country and leads Jerusalem’s inhabitants into spiritual prostitution and Judah astray. His influence spreads.

Arminian readers see a king using his authority to draw his people away.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of prostitution is a common prophetic picture of unfaithfulness to the LORD. This verse has no parallel in 2 Kings.

Reformed readers see leaders bearing heavy responsibility for the people’s worship. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, “the LORD, the God of David your father, says, ‘Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, nor in the ways of Asa king of Judah,
verses.arminianNotes:
A letter comes to Jehoram from Elijah the prophet, declaring that he has not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat or Asa. The letter appears only in Chronicles.

Arminian readers see God warning the king through his prophet.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text does not explain how the letter relates to the timing of Elijah’s ministry in Kings; interpreters offer different proposals, none certain.

Reformed readers see God’s word confronting the king. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not harmonize the timing.

verses.text: but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and have made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to play the prostitute like Ahab’s house did, and also have slain your brothers of your father’s house, who were better than yourself,
verses.arminianNotes:
The letter charges Jehoram with walking in the way of Israel’s kings, leading Judah into unfaithfulness like Ahab’s house, and killing his brothers, who were better than he. The charges are specific.

Arminian readers see personal accountability named plainly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The letter recalls the murder of 21:4. God has seen what was done in the palace.

Reformed readers see God as judge of hidden and open sin. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground about responsibility for idolatry and bloodshed.

verses.text: behold, the LORD will strike your people with a great plague, including your children, your wives, and all your possessions;
verses.arminianNotes:
The letter announces that the LORD will strike Jehoram’s people, children, wives, and possessions with a great plague. Judgment reaches his household.

Arminian readers see the consequences of a king’s sin spreading to those around him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The announcement is fulfilled in the raid of verses 16–17. The text does not explain how the people’s suffering relates to their own guilt.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment on a house. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not speculate beyond it.

verses.text: and you will have great sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels fall out by reason of the sickness, day by day.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The letter also announces that Jehoram will suffer a severe disease of the bowels. The sentence is personal.

Arminian readers see a warning that names the consequence of continued rebellion, though the text does not record any response from Jehoram.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator will report the fulfillment in verses 18–19. The notes do not elaborate on the illness beyond what the text states.

Reformed readers see God’s word certain to come to pass. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are beside the Ethiopians;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD stirs up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and of the Arabians near the Ethiopians. God moves the nations to discipline.

Arminian readers see God judging an unrepentant king through others’ actions (compare the box at Judges 9:23).
verses.reformedNotes:
The location of these Arabians is not certain. The Philistines and Arabians act on their own intentions while the text says the LORD stirred them.

Reformed readers see God governing the nations; Judges 9:23 treats the question. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: and they came up against Judah, broke into it, and carried away all the possessions that were found in the king’s house, including his sons and his wives, so that there was no son left to him except Jehoahaz, the youngest of his sons.
verses.arminianNotes:
The invaders break into Judah, carry off the palace possessions with the king’s sons and wives, and leave only Jehoahaz, the youngest son. The letter’s word is fulfilled.

Arminian readers see judgment falling as announced.
verses.reformedNotes:
This raid has no parallel in 2 Kings. Jehoahaz appears in 22:1 under the name Ahaziah; the text does not explain the variation.

Reformed readers see the Davidic line preserved through one son, as 21:7 promised. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: After all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease.
verses.arminianNotes:
After all this, the LORD strikes Jehoram with an incurable disease of the bowels. The prophetic word comes to pass.

Arminian readers see God’s judgment following the king’s persistent refusal to turn from evil, as the letter had warned.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator attributes the illness directly to the LORD, as the letter had announced.

Reformed readers see God’s word fulfilled exactly. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground, reporting the illness as the text does without elaboration or speculation about its medical nature.

verses.text: In process of time, at the end of two years, his bowels fell out by reason of his sickness, and he died of severe diseases. His people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
At the end of two years, Jehoram dies of his severe illness, and his people make no burning in his honor as they had for his fathers. His death is unmourned.

Arminian readers see public honor withheld from a king who did not honor God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ‘burning’ was apparently a funeral honor for kings; its exact nature is not described here. The notes keep to the text’s restraint.

Reformed readers see judgment completed. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years. He departed with no one’s regret. They buried him in David’s city, but not in the tombs of the kings.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoram, who reigned eight years, departs with no one’s regret and is buried in David’s city, but not in the tombs of the kings. His legacy is bleak.

Arminian readers see a life whose choices left no one mourning.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 8:24 says he was buried with his fathers in David’s city; Chronicles adds that it was not in the kings’ tombs. The difference is noted, not resolved.

Reformed readers see dishonor following sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
